title: Structural basis for alpha-actinin inhibition of cofilin binding to actin filaments
summary: Actin is a conserved cytoskeletal protein essential for morphogenesis, motility, and division. Its versatility arises from filament assembly and regulation by actin binding proteins. Among these, alpha-actinin organizes filaments into bipolar or unipolar networks, whereas cofilin binds preferentially to ADP-actin regions and forms clusters to shorten the half helical pitch (HHP). Here, we investigated the molecular mechanism of how alpha-actinin alters filament and protomer conformations and influences cofilin binding. Using high-speed atomic force microscopy, all-atom molecular dynamics simulations, and principal component analysis, we show that alpha-actinin crosslinking stabilizes actin filaments in the canonical helical state, thereby preventing the cofilin-induced helical shortening required for cooperative filament decoration. Stabilization occurs without significant changes in protomer twist and rise and subdomain geometry and maintains a flattened protomer conformation that restricts twisting needed for cofilin binding. Furthermore, myosin II (S1) and cofilin preferentially bind to normal and shortened half-helical structures, respectively. In contrast, the isolated alpha-actinin-1 actin binding domain mutant (ABD-E235K) and wild-type (ABD-WT) induce local transitions from the canonical double-helical filament to the single-helical protofilament, parallel-helical protofilament state (PPS), and nano-ring structures, while only weakly affecting cofilin binding and cluster formation on PPS. Notably, cofilin can bind and form clusters along single protofilaments without inducing helical-pitch shortening. Together, these findings reveal a mechanistically distinct function of full-length alpha-actinin and its isolated ABD and support a stepwise mechanism in which cofilin cooperative binding to canonical double-helical actin filaments requires initial binding to actin regions with shortened HHP, followed by protomer twisting and further helical shortening.

title: BiocPy: A Framework for Cross-Platform Genomic Data andMethods Interoperability
summary: Bioconductor provides standardized data structures and statistical methods for high-throughput genomic analysis in R, whereas Python has become a primary environment for machine learning, image analysis, and general-purpose data science. Combining tools across both ecosystems often requires ad-hoc file conversions or embedded language runtimes that can lose metadata, introduce maintenance overhead, or lead to subtle differences in downstream results. Here, we present BiocPy, a collection of Python packages that support cross-language genomic workflows through three complementary layers: (1) native Python implementations of Bioconductor's core data structures; (2) lossless data exchange via direct reading and writing of serialized R (.rds) objects and the language-neutral ArtifactDB format for persistent, multi-stage pipelines; and (3) a cross-platform method development paradigm built on shared C++ libraries wrapped across R, Python, and WebAssembly to support identical statistical analyses across environments. All packages in the BiocPy ecosystem are published to the Python Package Index (PyPI) with source code hosted at [https://github.com/BiocPy].

title: Convergence of Independently Established Oncogenes in a Combined Breast and Ovarian Cancer Model: Hub Gene Validation and identification of potential Food-Derived therapeutics.
summary: Breast and ovarian cancers share molecular alterations that may reveal common therapeutic targets. Here, we integrated six Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) datasets to identify shared transcriptional changes across the two cancers. Independent differential expression analysis followed by direction-specific intersection identified 396 shared differentially expressed genes (DEGs), comprising 192 upregulated and 204 downregulated genes. Protein-protein interaction analysis prioritized ten hub genes: AURKA, AURKB, BCL2, BIRC5, CCNA2, CDK1, FOXO1, KIF11, PTEN, and TOP2A. Functional enrichment highlighted cell-cycle regulation, mitotic spindle organization, and p53-associated signalling. Independent expression assessment using GEPIA2 identified seven hub genes significantly upregulated in both cancers, while FOXO1 was downregulated. Regulatory network analysis further identified candidate transcription factors and miRNAs potentially associated with these hubs. For therapeutic exploration, a 70,478-compound FooDB library was progressively filtered to 233 candidates using physicochemical, structural-alert, machine-learning-based bioactivity, and ADMET criteria. Molecular docking against eight selected druggable hubs, followed by decoy benchmarking and 100-ns molecular dynamics simulations, prioritized three complexes: CDK1-artonin L, AURKB-taraxacin, and KIF11-L-thyronine. CDK1-artonin L demonstrated the strongest overall computational support, whereas the AURKB and KIF11 complexes showed differing levels of binding and energetic evidence. This study provides an integrated multi-cohort framework for identifying shared molecular hubs in breast and ovarian cancer and prioritizing food-derived compounds for further investigation. The findings nominate CDK1, AURKB, and KIF11 for experimental evaluation.

title: A Shifting Landscape: Deconvoluting the Effect of Mg2+ and pH on Base Triple Formation in 7SK SL-1
summary: The small-nuclear RNA (snRNA) 7SK is essential for regulating the transcription of genes by RNA polymerase II through its interactions with Hexamethylene Bisacetamide Inducible Protein (HEXIM) and positive transcription elongation factor b (P-TEFb). High-resolution structures of 7SK stem-loop 1 (SL-1) reveal the presence of several base triples that coordinate the interaction with HEXIM. However, different high-resolution structures of 7SK SL-1 exhibit different conformations, each with unique base triple configurations. Previous NMR studies show that the conformation of 7SK SL-1 is sensitive to changes in pH and Mg2+ concentration. However, the exact mechanism by which Mg2+ and pH influence the formation and stability of base triples in 7SK SL-1 at an atomic level remains unclear. We combine molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, free energy calculations, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR), and small angle X-ray scattering (SAXS) to conduct a detailed investigation into the mechanism and dynamics of base triple formation in 7SK SL-1, and deconvolute the effects of pH and Mg2+. We find that the conformational landscape of 7SK SL-1 dramatically changes depending on the pH and presence of Mg2+, and that pH and Mg2+ act orthogonally to favor the formation of base triples. We discuss how the dynamic behavior of the base triples may provide a means for 7SK to regulate its interactions with HEXIM, modulating the transcriptional output of RNA polymerase II.

title: Integrating hydrogen-exchange experiments with conformational ensembles
summary: Protein conformational dynamics are central to biological function but remain difficult to characterise at scale. Amide hydrogen exchange (HX), measured by NMR or mass spectrometry, probes these dynamics but requires computational models for integration with structural ensembles. We benchmark models for calculating HX from ensembles using a large literature-derived dataset spanning folded and intrinsically disordered proteins. We then develop a model that identifies exchange-competent amides from local structural descriptors while accounting for electrostatic effects. The model predicts protection across a broad dynamic range in ensembles generated by molecular dynamics and generative AI. HX-guided ensemble reweighting improves agreement with independent NMR, SAXS, and folding-stability measurements. Millisecond HX distinguishes and refines alternative ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins, while reweighting of structured proteins reveals folding intermediates and low-population excited states. These results establish HX as a quantitative restraint for ensemble reweighting and provide a scalable framework for benchmarking simulations and generative protein models.

title: Evaluating WGS-based methods as an in silico replacement of phage typing for historical continuity and host association in  Salmonella Typhimurium
summary: Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (STm) poses a significant burden on public health worldwide. The Anderson phage typing scheme has historically supported surveillance, outbreak investigations and source attribution through associations between phage types and animal hosts. However, limitations inherent to the scheme have led to the gradual replacement of phage typing by whole-genome sequencing (WGS)-based methods. In this study, we applied statistical and machine learning approaches to 1,329 high-quality STm whole-genome sequences to compare phage typing with hierarchical clustering of core-genome multilocus sequence typing (HierCC) and the single nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) address. We observed low congruence (< 0.60) between phage typing and WGS-based approaches. Nevertheless, a random forest model using WGS-based subtypes as features was able to predict all phage types with high specificity ([≥] 0.94) and at least 80% recall for 10 of the 24 analysed phage types. These included phage types of human and veterinary epidemiological importance, including DT193, DT104, DT2, DT40, DT56, DT9, and DT99. We then assessed whether WGS-based subtyping methods could replace the host-association feature of phage typing. At higher distance thresholds ([≥] 100) WGS-based subtyping methods were more informative of animal host species and displayed stronger host-associations than phage types for 11 of the 12 animal hosts, with significantly stronger associations for ducks, finches, and pigs (all p < 0.05). Thus, despite low congruence between phage types and WGS-based subtypes, our random forest model accurately predicted several epidemiologically important phage types, including those important to public health and veterinary surveillance, supporting its potential as an in silico alternative for those phage types. Finally, our findings suggest HierCC and SNP address methods can capture the host-association information historically derived from phage typing.
